cells.tense: Here, with the pen, you are gathering what you think into one working order.
cells.act: act on the private sense of what is right
cells.ask: Where nobody else is watching or ruling — the small case waiting today. Settle it on your own sense of what's fair and do it, without checking with anyone.
cells.core:
The gathering is working. A dozen lines run through this, and they've settled into one order you can act from — a judgment is drawn, a chapter closed, the next thing can start clean because this one is finished. What's holding it steady is that you don't consult another's count. What's owed and what's fair, the small cases move through your hands without fuss.

Finish something concrete this week where nobody will see. An apology owed, an explanation owed — the plain call belongs to you, no second opinion needed. Give that one case the honest judgment and do it, once, without announcing it. The pen stays in your hand on the little ones, and that's where the larger order keeps its nerve.

cells.tense: Tomorrow's version of this sits finished in your head before any of it is real.
cells.act: do the next piece at the speed you can keep for a month, not the speed you can keep for a day
cells.ask: Tomorrow is already in your head, whole and finished, and you're running to make today's work match it. Take this week's share at a month's pace instead of a day's.
cells.core:
You're bracing at a future that can't be written into yet. The whole thing ahead is finished in your head — the entire flow in place, every move known, the ending already drafted — and the day's actual work looks slow against it. So the gathering turns into forcing: you write past the sentences that would tell you what the finished thing actually is, hurry whoever is working alongside you, and call the outcome before it has a chance to answer.

You don't lose that pace in your head. Keep it for the picture. This week, run the real work at the speed you could keep for a month rather than a day — the smaller, slower, even share. Then find out what the outcome turns out to be before you pin it down.

cells.tense: The work is finished and you have not crossed into what comes after it.
cells.act: stay with the quiet of it
cells.ask: Pick up the finished thing, or anything you love, and stay with the quiet of it for a while. Nothing gets planned, decided, or asked of the time.
cells.core:
The gathering has gone quiet. The lines that were once a strategy are sitting in a drawer, the pen is down, and what's next gets answered as a question without any crossing into it. You can describe the finished thing in detail; you don't move past it. The room you're in is the last room.

Don't force a plan or a feeling. Set aside a long, unhurried stretch with something you actually care about, and stay with the quiet of it — nothing decided, nothing pushed, no progress to show afterward. The weight shifts at whatever speed it shifts. You have done this once before without being asked to.

cells.tense: You have had the finished thing in your hands for a while and will say it came together by itself.
cells.act: share the joy with the people it belongs to
cells.ask: When something lands well, show the gladness to whoever was part of it — no speech, no modesty, no quieting it down.
cells.core:
The order in that thing is yours, and the account has it assembling itself. Anyone hearing it thinks it came together cleanly, and nobody corrects you, because the words carry. The finished version is real and in your hands, and the place where it was actually built isn't in the story.

Don't deliver it as an account. When the good moment comes, show the gladness with whoever was part of it, without shrinking it or saving it for later. Sit at the point where it leaves your hands, and let the plain gladness be what you pass along. You started this before anyone was watching; that same you is present now.

Reader's objection: 'it isn't that I haven't gathered it, everything's already decided and finished — the door closed.'
